rationale: A wins because it finds the cleanest uncomfortable story in the facts: "Airtable's agents can now update your records and draft your emails. It has not said how often they get it wrong." That is a real enterprise IT angle, not launch confetti. B is useful, but "Airtable just entered the AI agent market — that changes who it competes with" redraws a competitive map the update did not supply, which is how decent PR work wanders into fan fiction.
gaps_in_A: The valuation angle is honest but still thin: "Airtable's AI pivot is also a valuation story: private, $11B, and below its peak" needs a current mark, revenue, investor, or secondary transaction before it is more than a smart question.
The category angle leans on "widely known product," which is directionally fair for Airtable but not in the supplied fact block. Minor, but still imported context.

"If you want a stronger time hook for the category angle, run `newsjack-detector` first" is the right instinct, but it should say the pitch must die without a real external peg, not just get stronger.
gaps_in_B: "Airtable just entered the AI agent market — that changes who it competes with" invents the competitive frame. The update gives no named competitors, buyer comparisons, market-share shift, or analyst map.
"a company still marked at $11B" overstates the valuation fact. The update says Airtable was last valued at $11B, not that the market still marks it there today.
"all-in product pivot" is swagger pasted over a messaging shift. The facts say repositioning and agent launch, not a company-wide all-in bet.

B missed the sharper story sitting in plain sight: reliability and governance for agents that can update records. It mentions error-rate data only as a question, when that should have been a kept angle.
